title: From Promise to Practice: Closing the Application Gap in Quantum Computing
abstract: Quantum computing is a deep technology whose progress cannot be driven effectively from one direction alone. While the field has developed a growing catalogue of mathematically grounded algorithmic speedups, industrial impact will depend just as much on starting from real industrial decision contexts and working downward to what must be computed, validated and integrated. In this Perspective, I argue that sustained progress requires treating these two directions: bottom-up development from physics, hardware and algorithms, and top-down development from industrial needs and constraints. Equally primary and continuously coupled. This dual-viewpoint is not a matter of balance for its own sake. Quantum computers cannot solve arbitrary problems, so engagement with industry must remain anchored in algorithmic tractability. Yet tractable computations are rarely valuable unless they connect to decision points in established workflows such as candidate selection in drug discovery or the design of a new aircraft shape with improved aerodynamics. I analyse how historical narratives and structural separations of expertise slowed the formation of this coupling and outline what it takes to build it: explicit interfaces between technical teams and domain context and intermediate layers that translate quantum outputs into decision-relevant observables without suffocating foundational innovation. Framed this way, quantum computing's opportunity is clearest where deep physical modelling meets high-value decisions. Provided the field co-designs both sides from the outset.
summary: This perspective argues that quantum computing's progress requires equally developing both foundational algorithms (bottom-up) and direct links to industrial decision problems (top-down). The key challenge is building explicit interfaces that translate abstract quantum outputs into actionable, domain-relevant observables. This co-design approach is necessary for realizing transformative commercial value.
main_problem: The primary challenge is closing the 'Application Gap' in quantum computing, moving from theoretical algorithmic speedups to demonstrable industrial impact driven by real-world needs.
main_result: Sustained progress requires treating bottom-up development (physics/hardware/algorithms) and top-down development (industrial needs) as equally primary and continuously coupled.
method: The paper uses conceptual argument, analogy drawing from historical technological shifts (like classical computing), and analysis of required interfaces to bridge the gap.
model_or_system: The focus is on the computational ecosystem surrounding quantum computation rather than a specific physical Hamiltonian. It discusses algorithmic paradigms applicable to various industrial problems.
key_observables: Industrial impact; the ability of a technology to measurably influence real decisions (e.g., go/no-go choices, design trade-offs).
important_parameters: Algorithmic tractability; the coupling between technical capabilities and domain context.
main_assumptions: The success of quantum computing hinges on establishing organizational structures and interfaces to connect abstract quantum outputs to concrete industrial decision points.
figures_summary: Not specified in detail, but notes reference figures illustrating algorithm speedup spectra and simplified views of the Quantum Phase Estimation process.
paper_structure: The paper argues for a dual-viewpoint approach: coupling bottom-up algorithmic development with top-down industrial needs. It analyzes historical parallels to show how this coupling must be built explicitly through interfaces.
why_interesting: It provides a high-level, strategic framework relevant to all theoretical quantum physicists by framing the necessary intersection between fundamental physics research and applied computational utility.

The mathematical foundations of quantum computing place strict constraints on what can and cannot be achieved and any engagement with industry problems must always remain grounded in these realities.
